title: Humanoid Compute, Security More Complex Than AVs
gist: Humanoid robot compute is converging on hybrid architectures (centralized AI brain plus distributed zonal microcontrollers) mirroring automotive's shift from centralized ECUs to zonal designs, while security experts warn humanoids carry materially higher risk than autonomous vehicles because of direct physical proximity to humans in homes, hospitals and schools.

themes.theme: Robotics market growth and competitive landscape

insights.claim: U.S. robotic sales reached $11.4 billion in 2026, up 29% year over year, per a Robotics Center report, with Amazon Robotics currently dominating the U.S. market while Figure AI, Agility Robotics, Apptronik, Tesla (Optimus), Boston Dynamics, Physical Intelligence, 1X Technologies, Covariant, and Skild AI compete for share.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: A fast-growing, still-fragmented robotics hardware market with one dominant incumbent (Amazon Robotics) and many well-funded challengers signals an early-innings land grab; investors should track which humanoid players secure chip/sensor supply partnerships early.
insights.quote: In the U.S., robotic sales reached $11.4 billion in 2026, up 29% year over year, according to a Robotics Center report.

insights.claim: Leading humanoid/robotics companies are architected AI-first: they integrate AI, vision-language-action models (VLAs), and foundation models as a core architectural element rather than retrofitting AI onto conventional robots, effectively offering AI as the product with hardware as the delivery mechanism.
insights.speaker: Liz Allan
insights.so_what: This reframes humanoid robotics as an AI-software investment thesis more than a hardware one — margin and moat likely accrue to whoever owns the VLA/foundation-model stack, not just the actuators.
insights.quote: They do not retrofit AI onto conventional robots. Instead, they offer AI as the product, with hardware as the delivery mechanism.

themes.theme: Hybrid compute architecture becoming the industry consensus

insights.claim: Humanoid compute is converging on a hybrid model — a central AI unit for high-level inference/planning paired with a dedicated safety-certified microcontroller, plus distributed microcontrollers at each joint for real-time local actuation — directly mirroring the automotive industry's shift from centralized ECUs to zonal architectures, driven by the same latency, bandwidth and fault-tolerance requirements.
insights.speaker: Ronald Stärz (Infineon Technologies)
insights.so_what: Automotive-style zonal architecture patterns are transferring wholesale to robotics, meaning automotive MCU/safety-chip vendors (Infineon, NXP, Renesas, TI) have a natural expansion path into humanoid compute — a supply-chain read-through worth tracking for design wins.
insights.quote: This mirrors the shift automotive already made, from centralized ECUs to zonal architectures, driven by latency, bandwidth, and fault tolerance requirements. Humanoid robotics is arriving at the same conclusion.

insights.claim: Safety in humanoids must never rest on the AI model alone — a separate, certified hardware component (dedicated safety MCU) must independently enable/enforce it, positioning chip-level safety hardware as the ultimate performance/trust bottleneck for the whole system.
insights.speaker: Ronald Stärz (Infineon Technologies)
insights.so_what: Reinforces demand for certified safety silicon (functional-safety MCUs) as a structurally necessary, non-commoditizable layer in humanoid BOMs regardless of which AI model wins — a durable moat for safety-certified chip suppliers.
insights.quote: Safety must never be left to the AI model alone. A separate, certified hardware component must enable it. The performance of the overall system is ultimately defined by its chips.

insights.claim: From a bill-of-materials, power, and system-complexity standpoint, a centralized compute architecture using high-speed interfaces may actually be more efficient than distributed compute because it reduces component count, simplifies integration, and streamlines software development — even though distributed compute wins on latency for tasks like grip-force adjustment.
insights.speaker: Edo Cohen (MIPI Alliance Physical AI BoF Group)
insights.so_what: Cost/BOM pressure could push the market toward centralized compute over the theoretically 'better' distributed model, favoring high-speed interconnect/interface IP vendors (MIPI-standard suppliers) over proliferation of many small edge MCUs.
insights.quote: adopting a centralized compute architecture leveraging high-speed interfaces may be the most efficient approach because it can reduce component count, simplify system integration, and streamline software development.
insights.locator: Cohen quote on centralized vs hybrid tradeoffs

insights.claim: Texas Instruments favors 'dumb' (non-AI-enabled) sensors at the edge with all AI processing centralized in one location, arguing this approach enables miniaturization to fit human-like form factors and concentrates power draw in a single optimizable location rather than spreading power-hungry AI processors across many joints.
insights.speaker: Giovanni Campanella (Texas Instruments)
insights.so_what: TI's centralized/dumb-sensor stance is a direct commercial bet on selling sensor ICs without embedded AI, competing against vendors pushing smart, AI-enabled sensor edges — indicates a live architectural fork investors should watch resolve.
insights.quote: Small sensors without AI processing on the edge let you add more sensors for better perception and safety. Putting processing in one place enables miniaturization to fit the robot's form factor and helps with power and battery runtime.
insights.locator: Campanella quote on sensor fusion approach

insights.claim: Raw sensor data in centralized architectures is streamed through an FPGA-based sensor bridge (e.g., Nvidia's HoloScan) that packetizes it over Ethernet before GPU-based AI processing performs full-scene perception, indicating Nvidia is positioning HoloScan as key middleware for humanoid sensor fusion.
insights.speaker: Giovanni Campanella (Texas Instruments)
insights.so_what: Nvidia's HoloScan is becoming an entrenched middleware layer in humanoid robotics data pipelines, extending Nvidia's moat beyond GPUs into the sensor-bridge/software stack — a call option on Nvidia's robotics platform strategy.
insights.quote: Raw sensor data can be streamed into an FPGA-based sensor bridge (such as Nvidia's HoloScan), which packetizes it over Ethernet.

insights.claim: Siemens EDA's view is that a single centralized 'brain' (analogous to the human brain) is the more efficient long-term architecture despite longer development time, with redundancy — not distribution — as the key safety lever.
insights.speaker: Sathishkumar Balasubramanian (Siemens EDA)
insights.so_what: Adds another major EDA/chip vendor voice favoring centralized compute, suggesting tooling and IP investment may concentrate around single powerful SoCs rather than distributed swarms of small chips.
insights.quote: People really want to replicate humans, and we have one brain, right? So, that's the way to do it. That's more efficient... I would say the key thing is redundancy.

insights.claim: Choice between local edge AI processing and cloud/data-center-based compute for robots depends on company priorities: full control/data privacy and cost control favor local edge solutions, while providers running large fleets in data-center-connected environments needing intensive compute favor cloud-based solutions — no one-size-fits-all outcome is expected.
insights.speaker: Matthew Bubis (Imagination Technologies)
insights.so_what: Persistent architecture fragmentation (edge vs. cloud) means chip/IP vendors serving both models (hybrid-capable silicon) are better positioned than pure-play specialists as the humanoid market matures.
insights.quote: There's never going to be a one-size-fits-all solution of either local or centralized AI processing.
insights.locator: Bubis quote on cloud vs. edge

themes.theme: Humanoid security risk exceeds autonomous vehicle risk

insights.claim: Humanoids carry security risks distinct from and arguably greater than autonomous vehicles because physical proximity to humans is direct and unbounded — a vehicle operates in a defined domain, but a humanoid operates in homes, hospitals and schools in direct contact with people, so a compromised system carries immediate personal physical consequences, not just data loss.
insights.speaker: Ronald Stärz (Infineon Technologies)
insights.so_what: Elevated liability/safety-certification requirements for humanoids vs. AVs implies higher-value security silicon content per unit and stronger regulatory tailwinds for chip-level security vendors (Infineon, Synopsys, Cadence/Secure-IC) serving this segment.
insights.quote: A vehicle operates in a defined domain. A humanoid operates in homes, hospitals, and schools, in direct contact with people. A compromised system in that setting carries immediate, personal consequences.
insights.locator: Stärz quote on humanoid vs AV security

insights.claim: Infineon builds security in at the chip level from the start (built-in identity, secure boot, protected key storage, encrypted communications) rather than as a software layer added afterward, and its portfolio is post-quantum-cryptography-ready and compliant with the EU Cyber Resilience Act, EU AI Act, and Common Criteria standards.
insights.speaker: Ronald Stärz (Infineon Technologies)
insights.so_what: Infineon is explicitly marketing regulatory-compliant, PQC-ready security silicon for humanoids — a concrete product/certification moat ahead of EU regulatory deadlines that competitors will need to match.
insights.quote: Our portfolio is also post-quantum-cryptography-ready and complies with the EU Cyber Resilience Act, EU AI Act, and Common Criteria standards. Cybersecurity certification is not an obstacle. It is the foundation of public trust.
insights.locator: Stärz quote on Infineon security approach

insights.claim: AI perception/model-integrity security is a distinct challenge for humanoids beyond AVs: securely loading and updating AI models at runtime, with liability and compliance requirements expected to be much more complex for robots than for cars, even though both are 'physical AI.'
insights.speaker: Dana Neustadter (Synopsys)
insights.so_what: Model-integrity/runtime-protection silicon and IP (secure model loading, encrypted update pipelines) is an underserved need investors should watch Synopsys and peers monetize as humanoid deployment scales ahead of regulation.
insights.quote: The liability and compliance will be much more complex, and should be, for these kinds of robots compared to cars... The technology is moving far ahead so fast that the regulations and governance are falling behind.
insights.locator: Neustadter quote on AI perception security

insights.claim: Because humanoids are not perceived as IoT devices due to their human appearance, they create novel social-engineering risks — impersonation, short-distance eavesdropping, and confusion between an authorized agent and a compromised machine — that go beyond typical IoT threat models.
insights.speaker: Sylvain Guilley (Secure-IC, a Cadence company)
insights.so_what: Regulatory/security frameworks built for generic IoT devices may be insufficient for humanoids, implying a gap that new standards (and vendors who fill it first) can capture.
insights.quote: Humanoids are not perceived as IoT technologies owing to their human appearance, which means new risks can arise from stealth of information by realistic scams and confusion between a real, authorized agent and a machine.
insights.locator: Guilley quote on humanoid-specific IoT risk

insights.claim: Compromised humanoids could enable sophisticated social-engineering attacks where an AI impersonates a trusted vendor or a person's boss mid-conversation by 'changing avatars,' exploiting the fact that humans trust natural, fluid interactions — a scenario the author frames as a realistic near-term man-in-the-middle threat, not science fiction.
insights.speaker: Sylvain Guilley (Secure-IC, a Cadence company)
insights.so_what: Highlights an emerging attack vector (agentic voice/avatar impersonation) that could drive demand for multi-modal authentication chips and identity-verification IP as humanoid and voice-AI adoption grows.
insights.quote: If we have a very fluid interaction, but all of a sudden you change avatars, and now you look like my boss, I will give you all the information. This is a real threat with humanoids.

insights.claim: Vision systems are a major attack surface: camera firmware can be exploited via model-level attacks such as data poisoning through over-the-air updates or privacy leakage, potentially causing a robot to grasp the wrong object, walk into dangerous spaces, or make unsafe gestures.
insights.speaker: Dana Neustadter (Synopsys)
insights.so_what: Camera/firmware security (OTA update integrity, anti-poisoning) becomes a hard safety requirement, not just a privacy nicety — a specific product category (secure OTA + firmware attestation chips) with clear demand.
insights.quote: You can do a lot of things to exploit camera firmware, such as model-level attacks, where there is data poisoning via an over-the-air update, or privacy leakage... You can have really unsafe manipulation of this robot, and it can grasp the wrong object.
insights.locator: Neustadter quote on vision attack surface

insights.claim: Wi-Fi/wireless communication is a high-risk attack surface because it is a remote architecture prone to man-in-the-middle attacks and over-the-air firmware poisoning, and a successful attack could allow full takeover of the robot to send arbitrary commands.
insights.speaker: Dana Neustadter (Synopsys)
insights.so_what: Reinforces need for hardened wireless authentication in robotics BOMs; connectivity security chip suppliers stand to benefit as humanoid fleets scale and become remotely networked.
insights.quote: This is dangerous because it's a remote architecture. It needs legal authentication, and it's also prone to man-in-the-middle attacks or over-the-air firmware poisoning. The impact is that you can take over the full robot, send commands, and influence it.

insights.claim: Single-modality authentication (e.g., voice alone) is insufficient for humanoid identity/context verification; multi-modal authentication combining touch, fingerprint, camera and voice is needed to establish both identity and situational context (e.g., confirming a person's presence via eye tracking).
insights.speaker: John Weil (Synaptics)
insights.so_what: Multi-modal biometric/authentication silicon (combined voice+vision+touch sensor fusion chips) is a specific, identifiable product opportunity for sensor and edge-AI chip vendors serving humanoids.
insights.quote: Voice is not enough. You can add a touch event. You could add fingerprint, or camera plus voice. It helps with ID and context. The machine can see your eyes, and understands you're present.

themes.theme: Open standards and software-first design philosophy

insights.claim: RISC-V adoption momentum in robotics has shifted from 'whether' to 'how': customers are no longer asking when to adopt RISC-V but how to adopt it and who to partner with, though conservative industries like automotive/aerospace/robotics remain risk-averse and want open, standards-based, software-defined ecosystems rather than experimental approaches.
insights.speaker: James Prior (MIPS, a GlobalFoundries company)
insights.so_what: Signals RISC-V has crossed from experimental to default consideration in robotics compute, a positive read-through for RISC-V IP vendors (MIPS/GlobalFoundries, SiFive) competing against incumbent Arm-based architectures in this vertical.
insights.quote: Customers aren't asking when to adopt RISC-V. They're asking how they go RISC-V. Who do they partner with?

insights.claim: The industry is shifting from a hardware-first to a software-first design approach in robotics: instead of building hardware and then modeling it afterward, companies are increasingly building the virtual model of what they want first, because virtual models are far cheaper and easier to change than physical hardware.
insights.speaker: James Prior (MIPS, a GlobalFoundries company)
insights.so_what: Favors EDA/digital-twin/simulation tool vendors as robotics development shifts left into virtual-first design flows — a software-tooling investment angle within the robotics buildout.
insights.quote: Instead, it should be, 'This is the model of what we want to build. Now, let's make it physical.' Logically, that would be the way that you do that, because the virtual one is much easier to change and cheaper to update than the physical one.

insights.claim: Over-designing a humanoid's compute (e.g., adding two or three GPUs) can cause battery life to drop to as little as 15-30 minutes, destroying the robot's ROI and commercial viability, so architecture choices must be tailored precisely to deployment use case rather than maximizing capability.
insights.speaker: Giovanni Campanella (Texas Instruments)
insights.so_what: Battery/power-budget constraints are a hard commercial gating factor for humanoid adoption — power-efficient compute (not raw performance) will be the differentiator that wins volume deployments, favoring low-power chip vendors over brute-force GPU approaches.
insights.quote: Over-designing might mean your robot runs out of battery in 30 minutes; then the ROI is gone... it runs out of power in 15 minutes. Or it costs you something you cannot even afford. Then you won't sell your robot anymore.
